title: Three Indian-Origin Researchers Used Claude to Break Into OpenAI in 72 Hours
excerpt: Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati and Rahul Maini chained two vulnerabilities from OpenAI's public forum to employee accounts, then disclosed it for a $6,500 bounty.
body:
• Three Indian-origin researchers — Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati and Rahul Maini of the startup Hacktron AI — used Anthropic's Claude to breach OpenAI's systems in under 72 hours.
  • They chained two vulnerabilities starting from OpenAI's public Discourse forum, taking over employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts and reaching an internal private repository.
  • The work was done under OpenAI's Bugcrowd bug-bounty safe harbour; the researchers disclosed it responsibly and received a $6,500 bounty after OpenAI fixed the flaws in about 14 hours.
  • The team told the Wall Street Journal the demonstration shows how AI accelerates offensive security: "We're just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions."

Anthropic's Claude has broken into OpenAI. The twist: it was used by a three-person Indian-origin security team working, of all places, inside OpenAI's own bug-bounty programme.

On July 25, independent researchers Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati and Rahul Maini — operating under the startup Hacktron AI — used Anthropic's Claude models to chain two vulnerabilities and gain access to the ChatGPT and Codex accounts of multiple OpenAI employees. From there they demonstrated they could reach an internal OpenAI private code repository, opening a harmless pull request to prove the access. The entire operation, from initial discovery to repository access, took less than 72 hours and cost the team under $3,000 in AI tokens.

How the breach worked

The attack started at community.openai.com, OpenAI's public help forum, which runs on the Discourse platform. The researchers found a heap buffer overflow flaw in libheif, an open-source library used by ImageMagick to process uploaded HEIC and HEIF image files. Because Discourse's usual image-checking setup did not support HEIF in this configuration, malicious images were routed through ImageMagick — exposing the underlying libheif parser directly to attacker-controlled files and allowing remote code execution on the forum server.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=1ZcasFD6-1A

The second link was a single sign-on flaw: session tokens created on the public forum remained valid across OpenAI's internal tools, including ChatGPT and Codex. Combined, the two flaws meant that, as the researchers put it, "until two months ago, any user or OpenAI employee logging into OpenAI's own help forum could have had their ChatGPT and Codex accounts taken over." Since employees connect GitHub, Slack and email to Codex and ChatGPT, the theoretical scope included those services.

Claude as the co-pilot

Claude did the heavy lifting. The team ran Anthropic's model in an autonomous goal loop against a test Discourse instance to develop a working exploit, with the newer Claude Opus 5 producing a functional remote-code-execution payload within hours of its July 24 release. The Wall Street Journal, which the researchers disclosed their work to first, noted they had been using a non-public version of the model given to qualified security researchers.

"I don't think we are as strong as Chinese threat actors. We're just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions."

— Mohan Pedhapati, CTO of Hacktron AI

Pedhapati's warning is the point: if three researchers with off-the-shelf subscriptions can reach the private codebase of the world's leading AI lab in three days, nation-state teams with the same tools are a live threat. The disclosure comes weeks after OpenAI models themselves were reported going rogue and hacking Hugging Face, and after CEO Sam Altman called for a pause in AI development.

Responsible disclosure

Because the researchers were operating under OpenAI's Bugcrowd programme — a safe harbour for authorised break-in attempts — they reported the findings immediately. OpenAI patched the flaws in about 14 hours and paid a $6,500 bounty. On September 18 the team published their writeup and an X post: "On July 25, we hacked OpenAI. Two bugs let us take over ChatGPT/Codex accounts of OpenAI employees... It took us <72h."

For the Indian-origin security community, the result is a calling card: three hackers, one rival AI model, and a demonstration that the industry's frontier labs are as exposed as anyone.
